items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: Depreciation methods change reported profit, not cash
items.claim: A delivery van costs £40,000 with a 4-year useful life and £8,000 residual value. Under straight-line depreciation, what is the year-1 depreciation charge?
items.reveal_title: Straight-line: (cost minus residual) divided by life
items.reveal:
(£40,000 - £8,000) / 4 = £8,000 per year. Reducing balance would front-load the charge (e.g. 40% of £40,000 = £16,000 in year 1).

Neither method affects cash flow — the van was paid for upfront. Depreciation is an accounting allocation that matches cost to revenue across periods, governed by IAS 16. Different methods produce different reported profits in early years but the same total over the asset's life.
items.why: Profit figures are sensitive to accounting policy choices. Cash flow is not. This is one reason cash flow statements were made mandatory under IAS 7.

items.title: Ansoff said diversification was the riskiest growth strategy
items.claim: Igor Ansoff's 1957 'Strategies for Diversification' in Harvard Business Review introduced a 2x2 matrix. Which growth strategy did he flag as carrying highest risk?

options.text: Diversification (new product, new market) — combining product and market uncertainty multiplies risk

items.reveal:
Ansoff's matrix sequences risk: market penetration (existing product, existing market) is safest; product development and market development each add one source of uncertainty; diversification adds two.

Empirical work (Markides 1995, McKinsey 2010s) has supported this in aggregate: unrelated diversification destroys shareholder value more often than not. The 1960s conglomerate boom (ITT, Hanson) and its 1990s breakup vindicated Ansoff's warning.
items.why: Growth strategies look attractive on the upside; Ansoff's matrix forces you to articulate the downside risks for each route.
